paper_title: Mastering Diverse Domains through World Models (DreamerV3)
mechanism: DreamerV3 learns a recurrent world model (RSSM) in latent space, then trains actor-critic entirely inside imagined rollouts from that model. Crucially, three robustness techniques prevent scale-induced instability across domains: (1) symlog transformations compress extreme value magnitudes, (2) learned-rate balancing normalizes prediction targets by their own exponential moving statistics, and (3) return normalization via a percentile-clipping scheme keeps critic targets in a stable range regardless of reward scale — so the same hyperparameters remain valid across tasks with wildly different r
invariant: The agent never directly optimizes environment rewards; it optimizes predicted imagined returns inside a learned model. All domain-specific variation in reward scale, observation modality, and episode length is absorbed by the normalization and transformation layers, leaving the core gradient signal dimensionally consistent everywhere.
prediction: Removing any one of the three robustness techniques (symlog, prediction balancing, return normalization) while holding all else fixed should cause catastrophic performance collapse on at least one benchmark class (e.g., high-reward Atari or sparse-reward Minecraft), while leaving simpler, narrow-range domains relatively unaffected.
failure_mode: When the world model's latent space cannot capture long-horizon dependencies required by the task — i.e., when RSSM capacity is the binding constraint rather than numerical stability — the normalization fixes provide no benefit and the agent still fails, because imagined rollouts diverge from reality before useful gradients accumulate.
source_excerpt: Robustness techniques based on normalization, balancing, and transformations enable stable learning across domains... We find that the combination of symlog predictions, two-hot encoding with learned range, and percentile return normalization are critical for Dreamer to learn successfully across domains with a single set of hyperparameters.
